slides.title: Specializing The Structure For Efficiency
slides.notes: Open with the performance promise: geometric algebra should remain expressive while competing with coordinate code. Frame the lecture as a compiler story. Once the algebra, metric, object families, and recurring operations are fixed, the implementation can replace general multivectors with compact generated kernels and keep the generic layer as a reference.

slides.title: Where Generality Costs
slides.notes: Use the three pressure points as the reason specialization is necessary. Full multivectors allocate coordinates that many geometric objects never use. Runtime metric lookup wastes cycles inside tiny products. Generic product loops add branches and memory traffic exactly where a renderer or simulator needs predictable hot-path arithmetic.

slides.title: The Generator Contract
slides.notes: Emphasize that a code generator cannot optimize an informal idea of an algebra. It needs a written contract: dimension, basis labels, metric, specialized type masks, constants, and the operations the application will actually call. The more stable that contract is, the narrower and clearer the emitted code can be.

slides.title: Store Promises, Not Zeros
slides.notes: The storage visual should make sparsity feel structural rather than accidental. A vector, line, rotor, or normalized point is not a small multivector by luck; its type promises which basis blades are variable, zero, or constant. That promise removes memory traffic before the arithmetic is even considered.

slides.title: Hard-Code The Metric
slides.notes: Treat the metric as part of the compiled algebra, not as a runtime setting inside every product. The conformal example is useful because the intuitive null basis can be both more readable and more compact for certain objects. The generator should preserve that chosen basis while removing lookup overhead.

slides.title: Where Generation Can Happen
slides.notes: Walk through the tool chain without making one approach universal. Ahead-of-time generation gives inspectable library code, compile-time metaprogramming integrates with the host language, and runtime generation can adapt to observed calls and hardware. Each choice changes startup cost, debuggability, and profiling feedback.

slides.title: A Product Kernel After Simplification
slides.notes: Use the outer product example as a small audit trail. The high-level expression stays geometric, but the emitted kernel contains only determinant-like coordinate combinations and direct copies caused by a known constant coordinate. Stress that this is generated code first and trusted code only after reference checks.

slides.title: Constants Are Compile-Time Geometry
slides.notes: Make constants more than a storage trick. A pseudoscalar, a basis blade, or a normalized coordinate can act as a symbolic token that disappears during simplification. The important lesson is that readable geometric formulas can collapse to shuffles, sign changes, or copies without a human maintaining those low-level details.

slides.title: Specialize Whole Functions
slides.notes: Shift from individual products to whole expressions. If an application repeatedly applies a versor to a known point type, the generator can substitute argument types, expand products on the basis, simplify, infer the return type, and emit one straight-line function instead of a chain of generic calls.

slides.title: Outermorphisms As A Hot Path
slides.notes: Present outermorphism matrices as a representation change chosen for repeated work. A rotor sandwich is geometrically clean, but if the same transformation touches thousands of points or blades, initializing the induced matrix once can move cost out of the inner loop. The break-even point belongs to benchmarking.

slides.title: Nonlinear Functions Need Shape Guarantees
slides.notes: This is the caution slide. Linear products reveal their output support from input types, while nonlinear algorithms may branch on numeric values. Versor inverses and bivector exponentials specialize well when intermediates have fixed shape. General multivector inversion, meet, and join need fallback paths or runtime decisions.

slides.title: Design For The Processor
slides.notes: Tie the algebraic decisions to machine behavior. Compact storage reduces cache pressure, hard-coded metrics remove memory lookups, unrolled loops remove branches, and fused expressions avoid temporary multivectors. The goal is not clever micro-optimization; it is letting known geometry make the processor's job simple.

slides.title: Benchmark Complete Choices
slides.notes: Frame the performance table as evidence about complete representations, not a universal ranking. The ray-tracing comparison keeps the application fixed while changing the geometry model and implementation strategy. The lesson is benchmark-minded design: include conversion costs, hot paths, memory behavior, and the best traditional baseline.

slides.title: Carry Forward
slides.notes: Close by separating the two layers students should keep. The generic algebra remains the flexible reference model, useful for exploration and validation. Specialized code is the fast path for stable types, metrics, and repeated operations. Good implementations use both, with tests connecting them.
